articles.title: How QR Codes Store Data and Survive Damage
articles.excerpt: A QR code is a grid of black and white squares that holds text, plus spare data that lets a scanner rebuild parts that are dirty or torn. Here is how that works.
blocks: A QR code stores data as a square grid of dark and light dots called modules. It also stores extra backup data, so a scanner can still read the code when part of it is smudged, torn or covered. This article explains how the grid is laid out, how much it can hold and what the four error-correction levels mean.

Denso Wave, a Japanese company, created the QR code in 1994, and a team led by Masahiro Hara first used it to label car parts, according to Wikipedia. Ordinary barcodes hold a short number in one direction. A QR code spreads data across two directions, so it can hold far more in the same space.

Denso Wave holds a patent on the code but, according to the QR Code website, has waived its rights for codes that follow the published standards. That is one reason anyone can generate a code without paying a licence fee. The main international standard is ISO/IEC 18004. The QR Code website lists its first ISO version as June 2000, and Wikipedia says the current edition was published in August 2024.
The grid and its three big squares

A QR code is built from modules, the small squares. Sizes are called versions. Version 1 is 21 by 21 modules. Each higher version adds 4 modules to each side, up to version 40, which is 177 by 177 modules. The side length in modules is 4 times the version number plus 17.

Three large squares sit in the top-left, top-right and bottom-left corners. Each is made of nested squares in contrasting shades. These are called finder patterns. A scanner looks for them first, because three corner markers tell it which way up the code is and where its edges are, even when the phone is held at an angle. Larger codes also have a smaller square near the fourth corner that helps the software correct for tilt and curve.
The amount of data depends on the version, on the type of characters and on the error-correction level. The QR Code website gives these maximums for the largest size at the lowest correction level:

Digits only: 7,089 characters
Letters, digits and a few symbols: 4,296 characters
Bytes (for example, general text in 8-bit form): 2,953 characters
Kanji: 1,817 characters

Digits are the cheapest to store, because the code packs them tightly. General text costs more per character. A short web address needs only a small, simple code, while a long block of text needs a dense one.
Smaller codes scan more easily. A web address that is short produces a code with fewer, larger modules, which is easier for a camera to read from a distance.

QR codes use a method called Reed-Solomon error correction. The encoder takes the message bytes and works out extra check bytes from them using a mathematical formula. The check bytes are stored alongside the message. If some modules cannot be read, the scanner uses the check bytes and the readable bytes to work out what the missing ones must have been.
The standard offers four levels. Each level reserves a different share of the code for backup data, and the figure is the approximate share of the code's data that can be restored:

Level L: about 7%
Level M: about 15%
Level Q: about 25%
Level H: about 30%

There is a trade-off. A higher level survives more damage, but the backup data takes up room, so the same message needs a larger, denser code. A level L code holds the most data in the least space. A level H code is a better fit where the code may get scuffed, or where a logo is placed over the middle.
Why logos in the middle can work

Because of the backup data, a code can lose some of its modules and still be read. This is why some codes show a small logo in the centre. The logo hides modules, and the error correction covers for them. The covered area must stay within what the chosen level can restore, and the corner squares must stay clear. If too much is hidden, the scan fails.

The QR Code website notes a feature called structured append, which splits one message across up to 16 separate symbols. A scanner that supports it can join the pieces back together. It is rarely seen in everyday use.

The QR Code website also lists Micro QR Code, approved as a Japanese industrial standard in November 2004. It has just one finder square instead of three and is meant for small items where a full code would not fit.

Keep the data short when you can, so the code stays simple.
Leave a blank margin around the code. Scanners use the empty border to tell where the code begins.
Choose a higher error-correction level if the code will be printed on something that gets worn, and accept that it will look denser.
Keep strong contrast between dark and light modules.
These points are general information and not requirements from a particular standard. The details of margins and contrast are set out in ISO/IEC 18004 and in the documentation of the tool you use.

articles.title: How a Phone Touchscreen Senses Your Finger
articles.excerpt: Most phone screens detect touch by measuring tiny changes in an electric field. Here is how capacitive screens work, why gloves fail and how resistive screens differ.
blocks: Most phone screens sense your finger by measuring a tiny change in an electric field, not by feeling pressure. A grid of transparent wires under the glass is checked many times a second, and the spot where the signal changes is the spot you touched. This article explains that method, called capacitive sensing, and compares it with the older resistive design.

Wikipedia's overview of touchscreens describes two broad families. A resistive screen has two flexible, conductive layers separated by a small gap. Pressing the top layer makes it touch the bottom one, and the controller works out where. A capacitive screen has a transparent conductor on glass and notices when a conductive object, such as a finger, disturbs its electric field.

Resistive screens are cheap, work with gloves or any firm stylus, and cope with liquids and dirt. They need firmer pressure and are mainly used for single touches. Capacitive screens respond to a light touch and are the basis of most smartphone displays.

Capacitance is the ability of nearby conductors to hold electric charge. Two conductive surfaces placed close together, with an insulator between them, form a capacitor. The human body conducts electricity, so a fingertip near one of these surfaces changes how much charge it can hold. A touch controller is built to detect that change.

Wikipedia describes mutual capacitance as rows and columns of conductors that cross each other. The controller sends pulses along one set and listens on the other. Each place where a row crosses a column behaves like a small capacitor and acts as a sensing point.

When a finger is near an intersection, it lowers the capacitance there. The controller measures every intersection in turn and sees which ones changed. A grid with 16 rows and 14 columns would have 224 such points, according to one touchscreen maker's explainer, Nelson Miller. More intersections give finer resolution and let the screen follow more fingers at once.

Because each touch affects several neighbouring intersections, the controller can estimate a position that falls between the crossing points. That is how a screen can be sharper than its grid spacing alone suggests.

The second method measures each trace on its own against the ground. Wikipedia says it is more sensitive and suits single touches, simple gestures and sensing a finger that hovers nearby, but it cannot pinpoint a location by itself when several fingers are down. Many products combine both methods.

Pinching to zoom needs the screen to follow two or more fingers at once. Mutual capacitance does this well because every intersection is measured separately. Wikipedia names it as the main approach for tracking several fingers. Some resistive screens can do multi-touch, but they need many more connections.
Why gloves and water cause trouble

A standard capacitive screen needs a conductive touch. Wikipedia notes that gloves made of insulating material block the field, so the screen often ignores them. Workarounds include styluses with conductive tips and gloves with conductive thread. Some devices offer a high-sensitivity mode, which helps with gloves but can register touches that did not happen.

Moisture is another weakness. Nelson Miller says mutual capacitive screens are susceptible to moisture and suggests resistive screens for humid or outdoor use. A water drop can look like a touch to the controller, which is why wet screens sometimes behave oddly.

According to Wikipedia, E. A. Johnson of the Royal Radar Establishment in the United Kingdom described the first finger-driven capacitive touchscreen in 1965 and published a fuller account in 1967. At CERN, Bent Stumpe and Frank Beck developed a self-capacitance screen in 1972 and a mutual-capacitance one in 1977, and screens were in use in CERN's control room from 1973. A transparent resistive screen from Elographics and Siemens was shown at the 1982 World's Fair in Knoxville, and a University of Toronto team built an early multi-touch system the same year.

Wikipedia also describes surface capacitance, where only one side of an insulating panel is coated and the controller measures the change at the four corners. It is durable and has no moving parts, but its resolution is limited and it needs calibration, so it is mostly found in industrial controls and kiosks.

Resistive: two layers pressed together; works with gloves; needs firmer pressure.
Surface capacitive: corner readings; durable; limited resolution.
Projected, mutual capacitive: a grid of crossings; light touch; multi-touch; used on phones.
Self-capacitive: each trace alone; sensitive; used for simple touches and hover detection.

Phone makers do not all publish the details of their sensor layouts, so the exact grid sizes and signal processing in a particular phone are not public. The principle described here is the general one.

sources.title: How Do Mutual Capacitive Touchscreens Work?, Nelson Miller

articles.title: How a Helicopter Flies: Rotors, Pedals and Sticks
articles.excerpt: A helicopter's spinning blades are wings. Three controls change their pitch to climb, move and turn, and a tail rotor balances the spin. Here is how each part works.
blocks: A helicopter flies because its main rotor blades act as rotating wings. The pilot changes the angle of those blades with two hand controls and a pair of foot pedals, and a small rotor at the tail stops the body from spinning the other way. This article walks through each control and what happens if the engine fails.
The rotor is a wing that spins

An aeroplane wing makes lift as air flows over it. A helicopter gets the airflow by turning the blades around a mast. The more the blades are tilted into the air, the more lift they make, up to a limit. The tilt is called pitch.

The collective lever sits by the pilot's left hand. According to the flight-controls article on Wikipedia, it changes the pitch of all main blades by the same amount. Raising it adds lift and the helicopter climbs. Lowering it reduces lift and the helicopter descends.
Extra pitch also means extra drag on the blades. Migflug's explainer notes that the throttle, or an automatic governor, must add power to keep the rotor turning at a steady speed.

The cyclic is the stick between the pilot's knees. It changes each blade's pitch as it goes round, so a blade has more pitch on one side of the circle than on the other. The result is that the whole spinning disc tilts. Lift acts at right angles to the disc, so tilting it forward pulls the helicopter forward, and tilting it sideways moves the helicopter sideways. In forward flight, Wikipedia says, the cyclic changes the nose attitude and rolls the helicopter into turns.
Migflug adds a detail: because a spinning rotor behaves like a gyroscope, the linkages apply the pitch change about a quarter of a turn ahead of the place where the tilt is wanted.

The controls reach the spinning blades through a swashplate, which is a pair of plates around the rotor mast. Migflug explains that the lower plate does not rotate and is moved by the pilot's controls, while the upper plate turns with the rotor and passes movement to each blade through pitch links.
Collective raises or lowers the whole swashplate. Cyclic tilts it. The two can be combined.
The tail rotor and the pedals

When the engine turns the main rotor one way, the body tends to turn the other way. This is called torque. Most helicopters counter it with a tail rotor that pushes sideways. According to Migflug, the anti-torque pedals change the pitch of the tail rotor blades and so control heading, especially in a hover.

The collective affects torque, so a pilot who raises or lowers it normally adjusts the pedals as well. Wikipedia notes that some helicopters use a design called NOTAR, which replaces the tail rotor with air blown through vents in the tail boom. Helicopters with two main rotors turning in opposite directions cancel torque between them and need no tail rotor.

If the engine fails, a helicopter does not fall like a stone. A freewheeling unit disconnects the engine from the rotor, and the pilot lowers the collective at once. Air then flows up through the rotor as the helicopter descends, and that airflow keeps the blades turning, according to the autorotation article on Wikipedia.

Entry: lower the collective straight away so the rotor keeps its speed.
Glide: hold a steady forward speed; the article gives a typical glide angle of about 17 to 20 degrees.
Flare: at roughly 50 to 100 feet, raise the nose and apply upward collective to slow the descent.
Touchdown: land with a short run-on or, in some helicopters, stop and settle without forward movement.
Pilots practise this manoeuvre. Which procedure applies depends on the helicopter type and its manual.
Migflug states that Igor Sikorsky's VS-300 made its first tethered flight on 14 September 1939, and that its single main rotor and tail rotor arrangement is used by almost all helicopters today.

In forward flight, one blade moves into the oncoming air while the opposite blade moves away from it. Wikipedia says that at certain speeds this can cause the retreating blade to stall, which can make flight unstable. This is one reason helicopters have speed limits that are lower than many aeroplanes'. This is general information; real limits are set in each helicopter's flight manual.

sources.title: How a Helicopter Flies: Collective, Cyclic and the Tail Rotor, Migflug

articles.title: The Vespa: How a Wasp-Named Scooter Began in 1946
articles.excerpt: The Vespa was designed by an aircraft engineer for Piaggio and patented in April 1946. Here is how its enclosed body, direct drive and low floor made scooters popular.
blocks: The Vespa was a small Italian scooter designed by an aeronautical engineer, Corradino D'Ascanio, for the Piaggio company. Piaggio filed its patent on 23 April 1946, and the scooter went on to sell by the million. This article covers how the design came about, what made it different and how it spread, including to India.

According to Wikipedia, Piaggio engineers Renzo Spolti and Vittorio Casini built a prototype called the MP5, nicknamed Paperino, in 1944. Enrico Piaggio did not like its tall central section, so he hired D'Ascanio to redesign it.

Italy Heritage describes D'Ascanio as an aeronautical engineer who disliked motorcycles. It says he found them awkward, dirty and hard to repair after a puncture. It reports that he developed the first project in only a few days.

Wikipedia says D'Ascanio's MP6 put the engine beside the rear wheel and drove the wheel directly, removing the drive chain. It had a step-through frame, and the body panels were part of the structure. Italy Heritage adds that the gearbox was moved to the handlebars and that, instead of an ordinary front fork, D'Ascanio used a supporting arm similar to aircraft landing gear, which made wheel changes easier.

No chain, so less grease and fewer parts to wear.
A low, flat floor, so a rider could step through without swinging a leg over.
Bodywork that shields the rider from dirt.
A single-sided front arm that eases wheel changes.
The production scooter had a 98 cc two-stroke engine, enclosed and cooled by a fan on the flywheel, Wikipedia reports.
Both sources tell the same story. Enrico Piaggio saw the MP6 and said it looked like a wasp, "Sembra una vespa", and the name stuck. Vespa is Italian for wasp.

Sources agree that the patent was filed on 23 April 1946; Italy Heritage places this in Florence. Wikipedia says the scooter appeared in spring 1946 and was shown at the Milan Fair that year. It also says the first fifty sold slowly until Piaggio introduced instalment payments. Other web sources give different dates for the first public presentation, so the exact day is not settled across sources.

Wikipedia gives these approximate figures: about 2,500 Vespas in 1947, over 10,000 in 1948, 20,000 in 1949 and over 60,000 in 1950. Italy Heritage reports that the one-millionth Vespa was made in June 1956.

In the 1953 film *Roman Holiday*, Audrey Hepburn's character rides on the back of a Vespa driven by Gregory Peck's. Wikipedia credits the film with a large boost to sales and gives a figure of over 100,000, though that is one source's claim. Italy Heritage says the scooter became a symbol of freedom and Italian style, that it has been shown at the Guggenheim museums and that it is in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.
Foreign newspapers, including The Times, praised it as a distinctly Italian product, the same source says, even though some specialists at first dismissed it as a jalopy.
Innocenti's Lambretta was a rival scooter brand, according to Wikipedia. Piaggio also let other companies build Vespas under licence.

Wikipedia reports that Bajaj Auto licensed Vespa production in the 1960s. The licence was not renewed in 1971, but Bajaj kept building its own Chetak scooter. LML formed a joint venture with Piaggio in 1983 to make P-Series scooters and bought back Piaggio's stake in 1999. Piaggio returned to India at the 2012 Auto Expo without a local partner.
Dates and figures here come from the two sources listed. Web sources sometimes differ on exact launch dates, so treat them as the sources' accounts rather than a final ruling.

sources.title: The history of Vespa, an Italian icon, Italy Heritage

articles.title: How to Read the Numbers on a Car Tyre
articles.excerpt: A tyre sidewall code such as 205/55 R16 91V gives width, height, rim size, load limit and speed rating. This guide explains each part and the date code.
blocks: The string of numbers on a tyre's side, such as 205/55 R16 91V, describes its width, shape, wheel size, load capacity and speed rating. Each part has a fixed meaning. This guide decodes them one at a time using the examples in two public references, and it explains the four-digit date code that tells you when the tyre was made.
The size code, piece by piece
Goodyear's guide uses the example 205/55 R16 91V. Here is each part:

205 is the width in millimetres, measured from one sidewall to the other.
55 is the aspect ratio: the sidewall height as a percentage of the width. Here it is 55% of 205 mm.
R means radial construction. Goodyear notes that almost every new tyre today is radial.
16 is the wheel (rim) diameter in inches.
91 is the load index.
V is the speed rating.

You may see a letter in front of the size. Goodyear says a P, or no letter at all, points to a passenger car tyre. Wikipedia's tyre code article, which uses the example P215/65R15 95H, adds that P also shows the load tables follow the Tire and Rim Association standards, and that without an aspect ratio the figure is assumed to be 82%.
Multiply the width by the aspect ratio. For 205/55, that is 205 × 0.55, about 113 mm. A lower ratio means a shorter sidewall, which is why wide, low-profile tyres look thin from the side.

The load index is not a weight. It is a code that you look up in a table. Goodyear gives 615 kg as the figure for index 91. Wikipedia's example gives 690 kg for index 95. Each tyre carries its own rated load, and the vehicle's total is shared across four.

The letter after the load index is the highest speed at which the tyre can carry its rated load when correctly inflated. Goodyear gives 240 km/h for V. Wikipedia gives 210 km/h (130 mph) for H. The rating is a design limit, not a recommendation to drive at that speed, and speed limits still apply.

An ECE mark, showing the tyre meets UNECE standards for pneumatic tyres.
A maximum inflation pressure, which is the most the tyre can take, not the pressure to use.
TWI marks, showing where the tread wear indicators sit. The page says the minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm in most EU countries.
Original-equipment marks such as AO for Audi, MO for Mercedes or a star for BMW, showing the tyre was approved for that maker.
For the pressure to use, check the vehicle's manual or the label the manufacturer provides, as Goodyear advises, and not the number moulded into the tyre.

A tyre's age can matter as much as its tread. Goodyear says the production date is a four-digit code giving the week and year of manufacture. Wikipedia explains the longer DOT code used in the United States: after the letters DOT, the first three characters identify the plant, the next two are a size code set by each maker, and the last four digits give the week and year. Tyres made before 2000 used three digits.
For example, a final group of 2324 would mean week 23 of 2024. This is an illustration of the rule, not a reading of a real tyre.
Grades for wear, grip and heat
Wikipedia also mentions UTQG grades, which are wear, traction and temperature ratings for passenger tyres under the Uniform Tire Quality Grading standard.

Goodyear's advice is to match the load index and speed rating to the vehicle manufacturer's recommendations. The recommended size is normally listed in the owner's manual. This article is general information; for fitting and safety decisions, rely on the vehicle manual and a qualified tyre fitter.

sources.title: How to read your tyre sidewall markings, Goodyear
